title: Three-Axis Sorter
summary: Sort generic description cards onto three independent shelves: same receptor, same molecule, or reviewed-approved for the stated use — and notice when the evidence cannot settle the shelf.

items.misconception: The body's own hormone and a receptor agonist are the same thing
items.prompt: Card: 'A short-lived signal made by intestinal cells when food is present; it can stimulate the same cellular receptor as a manufactured agonist.' Which receptor shelf does this card belong on?

choices.text: Same receptor as the manufactured agonist
A different receptor from any manufactured agonist
choices.feedback: The card says it stimulates the same cellular receptor. A different-receptor shelf would contradict the card.

choices.text: The card does not say which receptor it uses
choices.feedback: It does: the wording explicitly names the same cellular receptor as the agonist.

items.explanation: Sharing a receptor is one observation. The body's GLP-1 signal and a manufactured agonist can act at the same receptor while differing as molecules. [1]
hint_ladder: Read the last clause of the card: what does it say about the receptor?
It names the same cellular receptor as the manufactured agonist.

data.card: A short-lived signal made by intestinal cells when food is present; it can stimulate the same cellular receptor as a manufactured agonist.
data.evidence: Source 1: both proteins work by stimulating the same cellular receptor.

items.misconception: Manufactured agonists are just the body's hormone under another name
items.prompt: Card: 'A manufactured medicine designed to act at the same receptor as the body's short-lived gut signal.' Which receptor shelf?

choices.text: Same receptor as the body's own signal
A receptor with no relationship to the body's signal
choices.feedback: The class is named for acting at that receptor. The card explicitly says 'same receptor'.

choices.text: There is no receptor mentioned
choices.feedback: A receptor is named: the same one the body's short-lived gut signal uses.

items.explanation: A GLP-1 receptor agonist is a manufactured medicine class defined by acting at that receptor; that does not make it the native hormone. [1]
hint_ladder: Look for the phrase 'same receptor' in the card.
Receptor agonist means the manufactured ligand acts at the named receptor.

data.card: A manufactured medicine designed to act at the same receptor as the body's short-lived gut signal.
data.evidence: Source 1: these medicines constitute a class called GLP-1 receptor agonists.

items.misconception: Every peptide signal uses the same receptor
items.prompt: Card: 'A hormone from pancreatic alpha cells that signals the liver to release glucose into the blood.' Which receptor shelf relative to the GLP-1 signal?

choices.text: A different receptor from the GLP-1 signal
The same receptor as the GLP-1 signal
choices.feedback: The card describes a different signal with a different target organ. Source 1 calls glucagon GLP-1's 'hormonal opposite' and says the two are 'clearly different'.

choices.text: Receptor cannot be discussed for hormones
choices.feedback: Hormones signal through receptors; the source describes which cells each signal acts on.

items.explanation: Not every peptide signal shares a receptor. Source 1 contrasts glucagon with GLP-1 as clearly different peptides with different effects. [1]
hint_ladder: Which hormone is described: the gut signal or the alpha-cell signal?
The alpha-cell hormone is glucagon, which source 1 contrasts with GLP-1.

data.card: A hormone from pancreatic alpha cells that signals the liver to release glucose into the blood.
data.evidence: Source 1: glucagon and GLP-1 are 'notably similar, yet clearly different'.

items.misconception: The native hormone is manufactured by a drug company
items.prompt: Card: 'Produced by intestinal cells close to the stomach and released only when stimulated by food.' Which receptor shelf relative to a manufactured agonist?

choices.text: Same receptor as a manufactured receptor agonist
A distinct receptor used only by body-made signals
choices.feedback: Origin is not receptor identity. Source 1 says the body-made peptide and exendin-4 stimulate the same cellular receptor.

choices.text: Origin tells us nothing at all, so no shelf applies
choices.feedback: Origin alone would not settle it, but this card is about the known body-made signal that shares the receptor.

items.explanation: This is the body's own incretin, described by source 1 as made by intestinal cells. It can act at the same receptor as a manufactured agonist. [1]
hint_ladder: Where does the body make this signal?
It is made by intestinal cells — source 1's description of native GLP-1.

data.card: Produced by intestinal cells close to the stomach and released only when stimulated by food.
data.evidence: Source 1: GLP-1 is produced by intestinal cells; both proteins work by stimulating the same cellular receptor.

items.misconception: A manufactured ligand cannot target a human receptor
items.prompt: Card: 'A synthetically produced molecule whose structure resembles the body's gut signal and which can stimulate the same cellular receptor.' Which receptor shelf?

choices.text: Same receptor as the body's signal
A receptor unique to synthetic molecules
choices.feedback: Source 1 explicitly says the two proteins work by stimulating the same cellular receptor.

choices.text: Synthetic molecules have no receptor target
choices.feedback: They can: the receptor-agonist medicine class is defined by receptor targeting.

items.explanation: A manufactured agonist can be structurally related yet distinct, and still act at the same receptor. [1]
hint_ladder: Focus on the last part of the card, not where the molecule came from.
It says 'same cellular receptor'.

data.card: A synthetically produced molecule whose structure resembles the body's gut signal and which can stimulate the same cellular receptor.
data.evidence: Source 1: exendin-4 and GLP-1 both stimulate the same cellular receptor.

items.misconception: A molecule that lasts longer must use a different receptor
items.prompt: Card: 'Related to the body's gut signal, persists longer in the blood, and works by stimulating the same cellular receptor.' Which receptor shelf?

choices.text: Same receptor as the body's signal
A different receptor, because it lasts longer
choices.feedback: Persistence and receptor target are separate observations. Source 1 reports same receptor plus a structural difference that changes persistence.

choices.text: Longer persistence rules out receptor comparison
choices.feedback: The card states the receptor comparison directly; persistence does not erase it.

items.explanation: Source 1 reports both facts together: same cellular receptor, different structure and persistence. [1]
hint_ladder: Does the card mention persistence or receptor in its final clause?
The final clause says the same cellular receptor.

data.card: Related to the body's gut signal, persists longer in the blood, and works by stimulating the same cellular receptor.
data.evidence: Source 1: same cellular receptor; a small structural difference protects the latter from digestion.

items.prompt: Card: 'A manufactured ligand that acts at the GLP-1 receptor; its structure differs from the body's own signal.' Which single shelf is settled by this card?

choices.text: Same receptor shelf — and that does not settle molecular identity
Same molecule shelf
choices.feedback: The card says its structure differs. A shared receptor does not make two ligands the same molecule.

choices.text: Reviewed-approved shelf
choices.feedback: The card says nothing about regulatory review; receptor targeting never implies approval.

choices.text: No shelf can be settled from this card
choices.feedback: The receptor shelf is settled: the card explicitly names the GLP-1 receptor.

items.explanation: One axis matches, the others do not follow. Source 1: two proteins share a receptor while their structures differ. [1]
hint_ladder: Separate the three questions: receptor, molecule, review.
Only the receptor is named; identity is explicitly different and review is absent.

data.card: A manufactured ligand that acts at the GLP-1 receptor; its structure differs from the body's own signal.
data.evidence: Source 1: same cellular receptor; small but significant structural difference.

items.misconception: The body's hormone is an approved drug product
items.prompt: Card: 'A signal made by intestinal cells when food is present; short-lived in the blood; no product or stated use is described.' Which shelf is supported?

choices.text: Same molecule as the body's own signal
Same receptor as a manufactured agonist
choices.feedback: The card never mentions a receptor or a comparison ligand, so the receptor shelf is not settled here.

choices.text: Reviewed-approved for a stated use
choices.feedback: Approval applies to products and uses. This card describes a body-made signal and states no product or use.

choices.text: All three shelves are undetermined
choices.feedback: The card is the description of the native signal itself, so the molecule-identity shelf is settled.

items.explanation: The native hormone is the reference molecule, not an FDA-reviewed product. [1][3]
hint_ladder: Which shelf has a positive match in the card rather than an absence?
The card describes the body's own molecule; review is a product-level question.

data.card: A signal made by intestinal cells when food is present; short-lived in the blood; no product or stated use is described.
data.evidence: Source 1: GLP-1 is made by intestinal cells; source 3: approval concerns drug products.

items.misconception: A product sold for a use has been reviewed for that use
items.prompt: Card: 'A version of a receptor-agonist medicine sold without FDA premarket review for safety, effectiveness and quality.' Which shelf does the card settle?

choices.text: Reviewed-approved for the stated use
choices.feedback: The card says the opposite: no FDA premarket review. 'Sold' is not 'reviewed'.

choices.text: Same receptor shelf
choices.feedback: The word 'receptor-agonist' hints at a target, but this card's asserted fact is about review status, not a receptor comparison.

choices.text: Same molecule shelf
choices.feedback: The card makes no molecular-identity comparison; a claim of sameness needs its own evidence.

choices.text: Cannot determine — no review information is given
choices.feedback: The card does give review information: it says premarket review did not happen.

choices.text: Regulatory shelf: not reviewed-approved

items.explanation: FDA says unapproved versions do not undergo premarket review; review status is a separate axis. [2]
hint_ladder: Which phrase in the card describes the review axis directly?
'Without FDA premarket review' — the card answers the regulatory question.

data.card: A version of a receptor-agonist medicine sold without FDA premarket review for safety, effectiveness and quality.
data.evidence: Source 2: unapproved versions do not undergo FDA's review for safety, effectiveness and quality.

items.misconception: Compounded means equivalent to an approved product
items.prompt: Card: 'A compounded preparation; the card gives no statement that FDA verified it for safety, effectiveness or quality before marketing.' Which regulatory shelf?

choices.text: Reviewed-approved for a stated use
choices.feedback: Source 3: compounded drugs are not FDA-approved and are not verified before marketing.

choices.text: Same receptor shelf
choices.feedback: This card is about regulatory status; no receptor comparison is stated.

choices.text: Same molecule shelf
choices.feedback: FDA explicitly flags 'is the same as an approved drug' as a claim needing scrutiny; this card does not establish it.

choices.text: Cannot determine — compounding status says nothing about review
choices.feedback: It does: source 3 says compounded drugs are not FDA-approved. That settles this shelf.

choices.text: Regulatory shelf: not established as reviewed-approved

items.explanation: Compounded drugs are not FDA-approved; the approval question is product- and use-specific. [2][3]
hint_ladder: What does 'compounded' tell you about FDA approval in source 3?
It is not FDA-approved, so the reviewed-approved shelf cannot be claimed.

data.card: A compounded preparation; the card gives no statement that FDA verified it for safety, effectiveness or quality before marketing.
data.evidence: Source 3: compounded drugs are not FDA-approved; FDA does not verify them before marketing.

items.prompt: Card: 'A small but significant structural difference from the body's gut signal; both act at the same cellular receptor.' Which shelf is settled about molecular identity?

choices.text: Same molecule shelf
choices.feedback: The card asserts a structural difference. Related is not identical.

choices.text: Same receptor shelf — but this card also tells us the molecules differ
Reviewed-approved shelf
choices.feedback: No product or stated use appears in the card; structure and receptor say nothing about approval.

choices.text: Nothing about molecular identity can be said
choices.feedback: A structural difference is stated, so we can say they are not the same molecule.

items.explanation: Source 1 supplies both observations in one sentence: same receptor, different structure. [1]
hint_ladder: What does 'a small but significant difference in structures' settle?
It settles that they are different molecules, even though the receptor matches.

data.card: A small but significant structural difference from the body's gut signal; both act at the same cellular receptor.
data.evidence: Source 1: same cellular receptor plus a significant structural difference.

items.misconception: A short-lived signal cannot share a receptor with a longer-lived one
items.prompt: Card: 'The body's signal disappears within minutes; a manufactured comparative molecule persists much longer; both stimulate the same cellular receptor.' What does this card settle?

choices.text: The receptor shelf matches, while persistence differs
Different receptors, because persistence differs
choices.feedback: Persistence and receptor targeting are separate observations; source 1 reports both in the same sentence.

choices.text: Same molecule, because they share a receptor
choices.feedback: The card says the molecules persist differently and source 1 reports a structural difference.

choices.text: Approved for the stated use
choices.feedback: No product or reviewed use appears in the card.

items.explanation: Same receptor, different structure and persistence — three separate observations. [1]
hint_ladder: Does the card talk about a product, a molecule or a receptor?
It compares receptor and persistence; no approval claim is made.

data.card: The body's signal disappears within minutes; a manufactured comparative molecule persists much longer; both stimulate the same cellular receptor.
data.evidence: Source 1: same receptor, GLP-1 disappears in minutes, the other persists longer.

items.misconception: A description of a molecule tells you its approval status
items.prompt: Evidence: 'A manufactured ligand acts at the GLP-1 receptor and its structure is stated.' Does this settle the reviewed-approved shelf for a stated use?

choices.text: Cannot determine: the product's review status and stated use are not given
Yes — receptor agonists are reviewed
choices.feedback: FDA describes unapproved versions of receptor-agonist drugs; receptor class membership does not establish review.

choices.text: Yes — the receptor shelf settles every other shelf
choices.feedback: This is the misconception the whole game targets: one matching axis does not settle the others.

choices.text: Cannot determine — unless the structure is identical
choices.feedback: The evidence has already stated the structure; the missing information is the product-level review status and use.

items.explanation: The evidence gap is product-level: which product, which stated use, and whether FDA reviewed that use. [2][3]
hint_ladder: Which shelf is being asked about: receptor, molecule, or review?
Receptor and structure are given; a product's review record and stated use are not.
items.review_note: Pending clinical review of the evidence-gap wording; the item asks only what information is missing.
items.worked_example: Ask: 'Which product, which stated use, and was that use reviewed?' Only then can the regulatory shelf be sorted.

data.card: A manufactured ligand acts at the GLP-1 receptor and its structure is stated.
data.missing_evidence: The product's review status for the particular stated use.
data.evidence: Source 2: unapproved versions exist; source 3: approval is a product-level verification.

items.prompt: Evidence: 'Two preparations both act at the same cellular receptor. No structure comparison is reported.' Does this settle the same-molecule shelf?

choices.text: Cannot determine: a molecular-identity comparison is missing
Yes — same receptor means same molecule
choices.feedback: Source 1's two receptor-sharing proteins have significantly different structures.

choices.text: No — they must use different receptors
choices.feedback: The evidence says they act at the same receptor; that part is settled.

choices.text: Cannot determine — unless we know the dose
choices.feedback: Dose is out of scope here. The missing evidence is a molecular-identity comparison.

items.explanation: Receptor sharing is one observation; identity needs a separate structure comparison. [1]
hint_ladder: Is there any structural information in this evidence?
No — a second receptor observation cannot substitute for a structure comparison.
items.review_note: Pending clinical review of the evidence-gap wording; no product data is used.
items.worked_example: To sort the molecule shelf, ask for structural information — not a second receptor observation.

data.card: Two preparations both act at the same cellular receptor. No structure comparison is reported.
data.missing_evidence: A comparison of the two molecular structures.
data.evidence: Source 1: same receptor plus a significant structural difference between two proteins.

items.misconception: Approval in general proves a particular use was reviewed
items.prompt: Evidence: 'A label mentions receptor-agonist medicines in general; no specific product or stated use is named.' Does this settle reviewed-approved for the learner's stated use?

choices.text: Cannot determine: a product-specific, use-specific review statement is missing
Yes — a class-level mention proves product approval
choices.feedback: Source 3 treats approval as product-specific verification, not a property of a class mention.

choices.text: Yes — the class mention identifies the molecule
choices.feedback: A class-level label does not identify one molecule, and this is the wrong axis anyway.

choices.text: Cannot determine — unless the receptor is named
choices.feedback: The receptor axis is not the evidence gap here; the question asks about review for a stated use.

items.explanation: Approval belongs to a product and a reviewed use; a general mention cannot settle it. [2][3]
hint_ladder: Does a general class mention name one product and one use?
No. Ask for the product-specific, use-specific review statement.
items.review_note: Pending clinical review of the evidence-gap wording; no clinical recommendation is implied.
items.worked_example: Name the exact product and the exact use, then check whether that use was reviewed.

data.card: A label mentions receptor-agonist medicines in general; no specific product or stated use is named.
data.missing_evidence: A product-specific statement about the reviewed stated use.
data.evidence: Source 3: FDA verifies safety, effectiveness and quality through a product-level approval process.

items.misconception: A sameness claim is evidence of sameness
items.prompt: Evidence: 'An advertisement says a compounded preparation is the same as an approved one; no comparative data are supplied.' Does this settle the same-molecule shelf?

choices.text: Cannot determine: comparative evidence is missing; FDA lists sameness claims as a red flag
Yes — the claim itself establishes sameness
choices.feedback: Source 2 lists 'claims such as the compounded drug is the same as an FDA-approved drug' among warning signs.

choices.text: Yes — the approved comparison product was reviewed, so both were
choices.feedback: Approval does not transfer to a different preparation; source 3 says compounded drugs are not approved.

choices.text: Cannot determine — unless both are receptor agonists
choices.feedback: The receptor is not the gap; the missing evidence is a comparative molecular identity check.

items.explanation: A claim is not data. FDA flags sameness claims; identity needs comparative evidence. [2][3]
hint_ladder: Is a claim the same thing as comparative data?
FDA lists sameness claims as a red flag; ask what comparison supports it.
items.review_note: Pending clinical review; framed as evaluating a claim, not judging any product.
items.worked_example: Ask what comparative test or structural record supports the sameness claim before sorting the molecule shelf.

data.card: An advertisement says a compounded preparation is the same as an approved one; no comparative data are supplied.
data.missing_evidence: Comparative structural or identity data for the two preparations.
data.evidence: Source 2: sameness claims are a red flag; source 3: compounded drugs are not FDA-approved.

items.prompt: Evidence: 'A signal is made by intestinal cells after a meal and clears quickly.' Does this settle any reviewed-approved shelf for a stated use?

choices.text: Cannot determine: no product, stated use or review record is given
Yes — because the body makes it
choices.feedback: Being made in the body is not a product approval. Source 3 connects approval to drug products.

choices.text: Yes — origin always proves molecular identity
choices.feedback: The question is about the regulatory shelf, and origin does not supply a review record.

choices.text: Cannot determine — unless the receptor is stated
choices.feedback: Receptor is another axis; the review shelf needs a product and a stated use.

items.explanation: Origin and lifetime are biological observations; approval is a product-level regulatory fact. [1][3]
hint_ladder: Which shelf does the question ask about, and what does the card actually describe?
It describes origin and lifetime; review needs a product, a use and a review record.
items.review_note: Pending clinical review of the evidence-gap wording; no medical advice is given.
items.worked_example: Name a product and a use, then check a review record — origin alone never fills that gap.

data.card: A signal is made by intestinal cells after a meal and clears quickly.
data.missing_evidence: A product, its stated use, and the review record for that use.
data.evidence: Source 1: native GLP-1 origin and brief lifetime; source 3: approval is product-level.

items.misconception: If it is marketed, it must have passed FDA review
items.prompt: Evidence: 'A preparation is being marketed for a stated use; the card includes no review record.' Does marketing settle the reviewed-approved shelf?

choices.text: Cannot determine — but only because marketing is forbidden
choices.feedback: Marketing is not forbidden here; the gap is simply that no review record was supplied.

choices.text: Cannot determine: a review record for that product and use is missing
Yes — being marketed proves premarket review
choices.feedback: Source 2 says unapproved versions do not undergo FDA review before they are marketed.

choices.text: Yes — marketing for a receptor agonist means the receptor shelf is approved
choices.feedback: Receptor targeting is a different axis; approval needs a product-level review record.

items.explanation: FDA explicitly describes unapproved versions being marketed without premarket review. [2]
hint_ladder: Does 'marketed' appear anywhere in a definition of FDA approval?
Source 2 describes unapproved products being marketed, so ask for the review record.
items.review_note: Pending clinical review of the evidence-gap wording; no product is named or judged.
items.worked_example: Ask for a review record for that exact product and use; marketing alone cannot answer it.

data.card: A preparation is being marketed for a stated use; the card includes no review record.
data.missing_evidence: The FDA review record for that product and stated use.
data.evidence: Source 2: unapproved versions do not undergo FDA review before they are marketed.
